newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Modest overshoot seen in UK PSBR-poll.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Modest overshoot seen in UK PSBR-poll.

text.p: Britain's budget deficit is likely to overshoot government targets modestly in the current financial year and in 1997/98, largely due to problems on the spending side, according to a Reuters poll of economists.

The mean forecast for the public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) in the year to April 5, 1997 is 27.9 billion stg, compared with the latest government forecast of 27 billion. Twenty-six economists provided estimates for the current year.
For 1997/98, the mean forecast from 27 respondents was 24.5 billion stg compared with a government forecast of 23 billion.

There is general agreement that a steady pick-up in economic growth should boost tax revenues this year and next, but economists say the perennial difficulty of reining in spending will be even more acute in the run-up to the election.

Alex Garrard, an economist at UBS, said revenue may be better than expected because of robust economic growth. But he foresaw problems on expenditure regardless of who wins the general election, due by May 1997.
"Central government departments are already overspending, as you would expect in the run-up to an election," he said.
"With public sector pay bodies queuing up for payouts under a Labour government, I think there is very little reason to expect spending to come under control."
The opposition Labour party is well ahead of the ruling Conservatives in opinion polls.

Garrard noted that even former Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher had been unable to prevent public spending growth from averaging over one percent a year. "These small percentages have enormous effects on the PSBR," he said.
Adrian Owens, economist at Julius Baer Investments, gave the highest forecast for 1996/97 PSBR of 30.3 billion stg, despite the boost he sees economic growth giving to revenue.

"The main reason why we are more downbeat is on the spending side," he said. "In the run-up to the election I think the pressures on the various government departments are going to be very great and as a result we'll see some considerable slippage coming through."
Whilst government pronouncements will be about the need for tight spending restraint, "they obviously don't want to upset interest groups in the run-up to the election," Owens said.
The PSBR should ease in 1997/98 as revenue increases and the new government tightens fiscal policy.
"Once the election is out of the way I would expect whoever gets into power to try to tighten up a little bit and make good some of the slippage," Owens said.
Whichever party takes power next year will find its room for manoeuvre severely limited by the size of the deficit, analysts said.
Economists at Lehman Brothers are more optimistic than the consensus about PSBR, forecasting deficits of 26 billion stg in the current financial year and 20 billion next year.
"We are pretty optimistic about the speed and scale of the recovery in the UK for 1996 and 1997, which should lead to rapid growth in revenues," said Robert Beange of Lehman Brothers.
